samples.text:
In many parts of the world, minority languages are disappearing because young people prefer to learn and speak the main language of their country or English. This essay will discuss the problems caused by this situation and what can be done to protect these languages.

The main problem is that culture is lost. Every language has its own songs, stories and traditions, and when nobody speak the language any more, these things also disappear. For example, old people in a village may know many traditional stories, but if their grandchildren cannot understand the language, the stories will not be passed to the next generation. Another problem is the relationship between generations. Sometimes grandparents only speak the minority language well, while the children only speak the national language, so they cannot communicate good with each other. In addition, young people may lose their sense of identity and feel that they do not belong to their community.

There are several things that can be done to protect these languages. Firstly, the government should support schools to teach the minority language, at least as one subject, so children can learn it from young age. Secondly, parents should speak the language at home with their children, because this is the most natural way to learn. Also, it is important to record the language, for example by making dictionaries, books and videos, so it will not be forgotten. Finally, media such as TV programmes and websites in the minority language can make it more attractive to young people.

In conclusion, the loss of minority languages causes the loss of culture and problems between the generations. I think the government, schools and families should work together to keep these languages alive for the future.
samples.why: Relevant problems and solutions presented · ideas stated more than explained · basic sequencing (Firstly, Secondly, Also) · adequate vocabulary · several errors in agreement, adverb form and articles that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
Across the world, many minority languages are in decline as younger generations increasingly adopt the dominant national language or a global language such as English. This essay will discuss the problems that result from this trend and suggest ways in which these languages could be protected.

The most significant loss is cultural. A language is not simply a means of communication; it carries a community's history, oral literature, songs and ways of seeing the world, many of which cannot be fully translated. When the last fluent speakers die, much of this knowledge disappears with them. Language loss can also weaken family and community bonds. In some households, grandparents who are most comfortable in the minority language struggle to have meaningful conversations with grandchildren who speak only the majority language, which creates a sense of distance between generations. Furthermore, young people who lose touch with their ancestral language may feel disconnected with their heritage and identity.

Several measures could help to reverse this decline. Governments can give minority languages official recognition and fund their teaching in schools, ideally through bilingual education in areas where they are traditionally spoken. Parents also play a crucial role, since children who hear a language at home from an early age are far more likely to become fluent speakers. In addition, making the language visible and relevant in modern life is important. If young people can find music, television programmes, apps and social media content in their heritage language, they are more likely to see it as something living rather than old-fashioned. Finally, linguists and communities should work together to record elderly speakers, creating an archive that can support future learning.

In conclusion, the disappearance of minority languages leads to cultural loss and a weakening of identity and family ties. Through education, family commitment and modern media, these languages can be given a better chance of survival.
samples.why: Clear position · cultural, family and identity problems extended with explanation · range of practical measures well organised · good vocabulary (oral literature, bilingual education) · frequent error-free sentences, one preposition slip.

samples.text:
Many of the world's minority languages may fall silent within a generation or two, largely because children are no longer acquiring them. The disappearance of such a language is not merely a technical loss; it has cultural, social and personal consequences, and while reversing the decline is difficult, it is by no means impossible.

At the broadest level, each language represents a unique store of human knowledge. Oral histories, poetry, traditional understanding of the local environment and distinctive ways of categorising experience are embedded in vocabulary and grammar, and much of this resists translation. When a language dies, this heritage is largely lost not only to its community but to humanity as a whole. The consequences are also felt within families. Where grandparents are most at ease in the heritage language and grandchildren speak only the dominant one, conversations may be reduced to practical exchanges, weakening the transmission of values and memories between generations. For young people themselves, losing an ancestral language can mean losing a vital link to their identity, sometimes leaving them feeling that they belong fully to neither their own community nor the wider society.

Efforts to protect endangered languages are most effective when they combine institutional support with community ownership. Official recognition and funding for bilingual or immersion schooling can give children fluency at the age when language is most easily acquired. However, schooling alone rarely succeeds unless the language is also spoken at home, so programmes that support parents are equally important. A language also needs a modern presence if young people are to value it: broadcasting, digital content and music in the language signal that it belongs to the present rather than the past. Finally, documentation through recordings, dictionaries and grammars provides a foundation for revival should the number of speakers fall further.

In conclusion, the decline of minority languages erodes cultural knowledge, family bonds and personal identity. Sustained investment in education, family use and contemporary media can give these languages a genuine future.
samples.why: Both parts sufficiently addressed with extended, insightful support · measures evaluated rather than simply listed · well-managed paragraphing · wide, precise vocabulary (resists translation, immersion schooling) · wide range of accurate structures.
